## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Gāmaṇicandajātaka* (Ja 257) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens with the verse incipit *Nāyam gharānaṁ kusalo ti* and is framed at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivers the discourse in response to the monks gathered in the Hall of Truth who were extolling his great, sharp, and penetrating wisdom (*paññāpasaṁsana*) [Fausböll 1879; SuttaCentral]. In the past story, royal education is depicted: Nalinaksha Dutt notes this Jātaka as an example of a Kṣatriya king personally instructing his son in the three Vedas and worldly duties (*tayo vede sabbaṁ ca loke kattabbaṁ*) [Dutt 1956]. The narrative relates how Gāmaṇicanda (also referred to simply as Canda) is entrusted with inquiries—including one from a tree deity (*rukkhadevatā*)—to present to the wise monarch King Adāsamukha [Fausböll 1879]. At the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the past characters, revealing that Gāmaṇicanda was Ānanda, while King Adāsamukha was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1879].
No cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan are registered with high similarity [DharmaNexus]. Textual reuse identified by DharmaNexus consists of five internal matches between the verse text and the prose commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), covering up to 392 characters [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the Jātaka in four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
